planting.note: Plant rooted stem sections or divisions in spring directly into saturated soil or very shallow water at a stream edge, spring, or pond margin in partial shade; brooklime roots readily from stem fragments and spreads by creeping, node-rooting stems.

directions: American brooklime is a sprawling native North American relative of watercress that roots naturally along the shaded, mucky margins of springs, seeps, and slow streams, making it a good match for a boggy, partly shaded corner of a Gulf Coast garden that stays wet through summer. Snip the thick, glossy, paired leaves and tender stem tips year-round in mild climates for a crisp, peppery, watercress-like green used raw in salads or wilted briefly into soups. Keep the roots constantly saturated or standing in an inch or two of water, since the plant declines quickly if the soil is allowed to dry out between waterings. Established patches spread steadily by rooting stems and can be divided and replanted at almost any time during the growing season.
sources: Native American Ethnobotany Database (University of Michigan)

planting.note: Scatter seed on the surface of bare, moist soil in early fall in a partly shaded bed; henbit germinates readily in cool weather and overwinters as a low rosette that resumes growth and flowers in late winter through spring.

directions: Henbit is a low, square-stemmed winter annual in the mint family that carpets shaded and partly shaded garden beds, hedgerows, and orchard floors through the cold months with scalloped, clasping leaves and small purple-pink hooded flowers. The young shoots and leaves have a mild, faintly sweet, slightly minty flavor and can be tossed raw into winter salads or wilted briefly into soups and egg dishes, much like a gentler, softer-textured spinach. It thrives in the dappled shade under deciduous trees and shrubs where few other cool-season greens perform well, and self-sows so reliably that a single fall planting typically renews itself for years. Harvest whole young plants or pinch tips regularly before flowering, when the texture is most tender and least fibrous.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall in a contained bed in partial to full shade; seed requires an extended cold, moist period to break dormancy. Plants form a low rosette the first year and bolt to flower the second year, so plan on a two-season harvest window and deadhead promptly to prevent unwanted spread.

directions: Garlic mustard is a biennial woodland-edge herb whose first-year rosette of scalloped, dark-green leaves carries a distinctive garlic-and-mustard bite that makes it a useful, unusually shade-tolerant flavoring green for a food forest understory. Harvest the mild, tender first-year leaves for pesto, chopped salads, and sauteed greens, then gather the young second-year flower shoots in spring before the small white flowers open, when they can be cooked like a peppery broccoli raab. Because it self-sows aggressively and is classified as invasive in much of eastern North America, grow it only in a contained raised bed or large container and remove flowering stalks before seed set to keep it from escaping into nearby woodland. A single planting in a partly shaded bed typically self-perpetuates for years with no further sowing needed.
sources: Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions in spring into consistently wet soil or very shallow water (up to 2 inches deep) at a pond margin, rain garden, or bog bed in partial shade; this variegated sport does not come reliably true from seed and is propagated exclusively by division.

directions: 'Flamingo' is a compact, boldly variegated sport of water celery, its narrow leaves splashed in pink, cream, and green rather than the plain green of the wild species, making it a dual-purpose plant for the edge of a shaded pond or rain garden bed. The tender young stems and leaves carry the same crisp, mild parsley-celery flavor used fresh in Korean and Japanese cooking and can be snipped regularly for salads, garnishes, and cold noodle dishes. Because the color is brightest in cooler weather and with some direct morning sun, site it where it gets a few hours of light before afternoon shade takes over in a hot Gulf Coast summer. Divide congested clumps every year or two in spring to maintain vigorous color and prevent the planting from reverting toward plain green foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct sow or allow self-sown seedlings to establish in moist, disturbed soil in partial shade after the last frost; lady's thumb germinates readily in warm soil and grows quickly through summer in damp, dappled-light spots such as the edge of a vegetable bed or rain garden.

directions: Lady's thumb is a sprawling summer annual in the knotweed family, easily identified by the dark, thumbprint-shaped smudge on each narrow leaf and the small, bottlebrush-like pink flower spikes it produces from midsummer into fall. The young leaves and tender stem tips have a mild, slightly peppery flavor similar to a soft watercress and can be added raw to salads or cooked briefly as a potherb, though larger, older leaves turn tougher and are better cooked. It thrives in the moist, partly shaded, disturbed soil found at the edge of vegetable beds, compost areas, and rain gardens where few deliberately planted greens compete well, and self-sows freely once established. Harvest continuously through summer by pinching tips, which also helps limit how much the plant spreads by seed.
